Code by Example: Counters

A counter is the smallest program that still has state worth reading. This page builds one step by step, so every fragment on the right is short enough to follow on its own while the text on the left says why it is written that way.

The counter keeps its running total in a field and grows it by a fixed step, so the same value always produces the same sequence however often the program is run.

 
func count(step int) int {
    total := 0
    for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
        total += step
    }
    return total
}

Calling it twice with different steps shows that nothing is shared between calls: each call starts again from zero, which is the property the next example takes away on purpose.

 
    fmt.Println(count(2))
 
$ go run counters.go
6

A counter that has to remember its total between calls needs somewhere to keep it, and the choice of that place is what the next example is about. Until then, the function above is the whole idea: a loop, a running total and a value handed back to the caller once the loop is done.
